highlights.text: You must know how that intro goes. When they wheel U-6389 out? And do that thing in front of you, that’s completely impossible? Jesus. They gave us all an hour to try it out ourselves, try to figure out the trick. But there isn’t a trick. It’s just…an error in the universe. A gap. Science doesn’t apply. Physics and biology go on vacation. It’s messed up.”

And there’s definitely something wrong with him now because he’s visible through the tables, like an augmented reality holoprojection jammed inside Lee’s eyeball. Lee realizes with a stab of fear that he can even see Gage when he blinks. His eyelids close, but Gage is still there, an apparition in what for all of Lee’s life has been totally personal, private darkness.

The database entry that you are currently reading is created and maintained by victims of U-7175, because it is only visible to victims of U-7175. If you are reading this entry, U-7175 has caught you.

You have between 15 minutes and 2 hours to reach UO Wyeleigh, basement level 8, laboratory 703, then familiarize yourself with the existing research, and continue this research until you find a way to contain or neutralize U-7175, or, more likely, die. If your field of expertise is not related to antimemetic containment, we sincerely apologize, and advise you to start learning. Fast.

There are dozens of separate lines of research, contributed in patchwork by a succession of victims, all ending with variations on the same final line: “I’m going to try X. If you’re reading this, X didn’t work and I’m dead, which means approach X is a dead end, and you have to think of something else.”

More than a hundred people, most of them apparently possessing doctorates, have slid into the maw of this thing, fought briefly, and, with a greater or lesser degree of dignity, died. There are no remaining untried threads. “I’m fucked!” Lee concludes.

Then he remembers who he is, and where he is, and what his responsibilities are. He goes to the computer, to the Unknown entry, adds himself to the victim tally, and writes up exactly what it is he’s about to try. Because he might not be the last one, and the world needs to know that this didn’t work.
X’s restorative effect on the human memory is essentially a side effect. However, this side effect is so useful that it has become the drug’s main practical purpose.

“We got looped. It was textbook. We built the unthinkable bomb, took it to Skye and test-detonated it…and it worked perfectly. The bomb destroyed itself, and erased its own successful detonation, and flattened all the knowledge that had gone together to build it. We forgot that we had ever built the bomb at all, and started over.
It was the opposite of unthinkable; it was unforgettable.
The more you know about it, the more it knows about you. If you can see it, it can see you. And it hates to be seen.”
There’s another conglomeration of severed fingers in the last room, coating the room’s interior like the innards of an exploded elephant.
The world was like some grand unbalanced equation, with known science on one side and all these Unknowns on the other.
“You will feel this for the rest of your life. Every day, you will wake up with a sick cold feeling in your stomach where there used to be a real life. And you’ll wonder why.”
Asynchronous research—whereby the research topic is forgotten entirely between iterations, and rediscovered over and over—is a perfectly standard practice in the Antimemetics Division,

Those data points are points on U-3125’s hull; those manifestations are the shadows it casts on our reality. You link four or five different Unknowns together into a single shape, and you see it…And it sees you…”

Now that she knows it’s there, she can feel it like cosmic radiation, boring holes in the world with its manifestations and effortlessly silencing anybody who recognizes the larger pattern. It is not of reality, not of humanity; human thought cannot coexist with it. It is from a higher, worse place, and it is descending.

Because that’s all you can do when you see U-3125: run away and try to forget what you saw…seek oblivion in chemicals, or alcohol, or head trauma. And even that can’t work every time. It’s circling in. We meet it over and over again and we don’t realize it. There’s no way we can stop ourselves from rediscovering it! We’re too damned smart!”
“Ideas can be killed,” she says, stepping into the airlock. “How?” “With better ideas.”
Human civilization will be entirely eradicated as an abstract concept and replaced with something unimaginably worse.
I’ve survived too long. I forgot which universe this was. For a while there, I thought, maybe…this was the universe where we win sometimes.
Go home tonight and drink that champagne. The whole bottle. Become incapable and unbalanced. Do this in my honor. The special occasion will be that the world has not fucking ended.

if you extend that concept from mathematics to the real world you get an assertion that some physical realities are just going to be there and scientifically unjustifiable. Inexplicabilities. Like there’s going to be a wall we hit one day, where all the remaining Unknowns are just going to be fixtures, permanently Unknowable, and we’ll have two options: give up and live our lives, or die trying and failing to know them.
“The Organization motto is ‘Freedom means no fear.’ If there are no humans, there is no fear. Job done.” “But also no freedom,” Devlin says. He has a thin, reedy voice. “The dead aren’t free—”
He would need to design and build the box while already inside the box he was building. He would need to box the universe.
“The Organization no longer believes in unsolvable problems,” he says. “Congratulations on your promotion to chief of Antimemetics.
If it feels like everything is fine, that’s how you know you’re dying.
He can make it. He can lock himself in. He’s going to miss the sky. It hurts to think. But he can think.
“These things happen. And we say to ourselves, ‘Never again.’ And a hundred years pass. And they happen. Again.”
